The Triassic period, which lasted from approximately 252 to 201 million years ago, marked the beginning of the Mesozoic era. The half-way point of the Triassic occurred around 226-227 million years ago, during what geologists call the Late Triassic epoch.

This period was characterized by significant evolutionary developments, particularly among early dinosaurs and various marine organisms. The supercontinent Pangaea was still intact, though early signs of rifting were beginning to appear. The climate was generally hot and dry, with strong seasonal variations.

Around this mid-point, various important species were emerging, including some of the earliest true mammals. The oceans were recovering from the devastating Permian-Triassic extinction event, with ammonoids and marine reptiles becoming increasingly diverse. The first pterosaurs were also appearing during this time, marking the beginning of vertebrate flight.

The vegetation during this period was dominated by seed ferns and early cycads, though the first magnolias had begun to appear, marking a crucial development in flowering plant evolution. The atmospheric oxygen levels were steadily increasing, reaching about 23%, which contributed to the success of various animal groups, particularly the early archosaurs that would later give rise to modern crocodiles and birds.

The Triassic Period, which lasted from approximately 252 to 201 million years ago, marked the beginning of the Mesozoic Era. The halfway point of the Triassic occurred around 227 million years ago, during what geologists call the Ladinian-Carnian boundary.

This middle Triassic period was characterized by the continued diversification of marine life and the emergence of early dinosaur species. The supercontinent Pangaea was fully assembled at this time, creating vast desert environments in the interior and seasonal monsoon conditions along the coasts.

The atmosphere during this period contained significantly higher levels of carbon dioxide than today, with oxygen levels around 15%. The middle Triassic saw the evolution of the first pterosaurs and the emergence of the earliest mammals, particularly the cynodont group. Marine reptiles like ichthyosaurs reached their peak diversity during this time, while the first coral reefs composed primarily of scleractinian corals began forming in the Tethys Ocean.

The vegetation during this period was dominated by seed ferns and early conifers, with the first appearances of cycads starting to emerge in the tropical regions. The earliest known flowering plants also began to appear during this time, though they remained relatively rare until the late Jurassic period.

The Triassic Period, which lasted from approximately 252 to 201 million years ago, marked the beginning of the Mesozoic Era. The halfway point of the Triassic occurred around 226.5 million years ago, during what geologists call the Late Triassic epoch.

This middle period was characterized by the continued dominance of synapsids and the early emergence of dinosaurs. The climate during this time was generally hot and dry, with much of the supercontinent Pangaea experiencing seasonal monsoons. The oceans were recovering from the devastating Permian-Triassic extinction event, with new marine species beginning to flourish.

The halfway point of the Triassic saw the emergence of the first primitive pterosaurs, which would later become the dominant flying vertebrates. This period also witnessed the evolution of the earliest mammals, particularly the cynodont group, which began developing specialized teeth and enhanced hearing capabilities. The first coral reefs since the Permian extinction were starting to form, primarily built by the now-extinct scleractinian species Parasaurolophus maeandrina, which created distinctive honeycomb-like structures that can still be found in fossil beds throughout modern-day Europe and North Africa.
